subject: political-science
readings: OD ch. 5 (Orvis & Drogus, *Governing Institutions in Democracies*)

cards.back: Executive and legislature are **fused**: parliament chooses the chief executive (**PM**), who is both the majority party leader and a sitting legislator. A **ceremonial head of state** stays out of politics.

Executive and legislature are **elected separately with separate powers** (the **separation of powers**). The president is **directly elected** and serves a **fixed term**; branches generally cannot remove each other.
cards.hint: Separation of powers; directly elected, fixed term.

cards.back: Executive power is **split**: a **directly elected president** (head of state, with real powers) plus a **PM** (head of government) backed by the parliamentary majority. Originated in France in 1958.

cards.front: Compare parliamentary, presidential, and semi presidential systems on powers, how the executive is chosen, and removal.
cards.back: **Powers:** fused · separated · split. **Chosen:** parliament names PM · president directly elected · president elected and PM named by parliament. **Removed:** vote of no confidence · impeachment only · PM by no confidence while president keeps a fixed term.

Majoritarian **concentrates power**: single party executive, dominant over the legislature, unicameral, flexible constitution → **few veto players**. Consensus **disperses power**: coalition executives, balanced branches, bicameral, rigid constitution → **many veto players**.

cards.front: Which concept means any actor whose agreement is needed to change policy?
According to Tsebelis, how does adding veto players change policy?
cards.back: **Less policy change.** Each player prefers a set of policies over the **status quo**; a new policy passes only if it sits inside **every** player's set (the **winset**). 1) More players shrink the winset. 2) Greater **ideological distance** between them shrinks it further → gridlock.
cards.hint: More players → smaller winset → less change.

cards.back: The principle that the executive, legislature, and judiciary are **elected or constituted separately and hold separate powers**, so each can check the others. It is the defining feature of presidentialism.
cards.hint: Separate branches that check each other.

cards.front: How is a PM removed through a **vote of no confidence**?
cards.back: Parliament votes that it no longer backs the PM. The PM then either 1) resigns, so the party picks a new leader, or 2) asks the head of state to call **new elections**; the PM may instead **dissolve** parliament. Such votes succeed only about **5%** of the time, but even losing one signals fatal weakness.
cards.hint: No confidence → resign or new elections.

cards.front: What are **Linz's** three perils of presidentialism?
cards.back: 1) **Dual legitimacy:** two independently elected branches with no democratic tie breaker. 2) **Winner take all:** presidents over read their mandate and refuse to compromise. 3) **Inflexible fixed terms:** a failing president cannot be removed. His claim: presidentialism is inherently crisis prone (*The Perils of Presidentialism*, 1990).
cards.hint: Dual legitimacy · winner take all · fixed terms.

cards.front: How do **unitary** and **federal** systems differ on sovereignty?
cards.back: 1) **Unitary:** the centre holds **sole sovereignty**, and local powers are **delegated and revocable**. 2) **Federal:** sovereignty is **constitutionally shared** with subunits, which limits majorities, protects minorities, and adds **veto players**.

cards.front: What is **cohabitation** in a semi presidential system?
cards.back: When the president and the legislative majority come from **different parties**. The president must appoint a **PM from the opposing majority** and retreat to their own domain: 1) the president runs foreign policy and defence, 2) the PM runs domestic policy.
